Tensor Analysis – Practical 6 Solutions Information: • Please make sure to complete all exercises before the next lecture. • The exercises marked with [See lecture] were solved in class. • The exercises are not organised by difficulty. 6.1 Using the alternative definitions of Lk i′ and Li′ k i.e., L k i′ = ∂xk ∂x′i , L i′ k = ∂x′i ∂xk , show that Li k′L k′ j = δi .j, where here δi .j is the usual Kronecker delta, but just written according to the notation in generalised coordinate systems. Solution: We have L i k′L k′ j = ∂xi ∂x′k ∂x′k ∂xj = ∂xi ∂xj = δi .j, as required. 6.2 [See Lecture] Let Aikℓ be a covariant tensor of order 3 and Bpqmn a contravariant tensor of order 4. Prove that AikℓBkℓmn is a mixed tensor of order 3 (with one covariant and two contravariant indices). Solution: As Aikℓ is a covariant tensor and Bpqmn is a contravariant tensor, we have A′ ikℓ = L p i′L q k′L r ℓ′Apqr and B′kℓmn = L k′ s L ℓ′ t L m′ u L n′ v Bstuv. 1

# Page 2^page=2
2 Hence (AikℓBkℓmn) ′ = A′ ikℓB′kℓmn = L p i′L q k′L r ℓ′ApqrL k′ s L ℓ′ t L m′ u L n′ v Bstuv = L p i′(L q k′L k′ s )(L r ℓ′L ℓ′ t )Lm′ u L n′ v ApqrBstuv = L p i′(δq .s)(δr .t)Lm′ u L n′ v ApqrBstuv (using Question 1) = L p i′L m′ u L n′ v ApqrBqruv, which shows that AikℓBkℓmn is a mixed tensor with one covariant and two contravariant indices, as required. 6.3 Which of the following relations between associated tensors are correct? Explain. (1) T p q = gr pTrq, (2) Spq = grpgsqSrs, (3) W p ·rs = gsqW pq ··s , (4) V qm·tk ··n = gpkgsngrmV q·st ·r··p. Solution: None of them. In (1), a dot is missing in one suffix. This is necessary to specify the order of occurrence of indices. We also need to raise r and call it p. The correct expression is T p ·q = grpTrq. In (2), we see that s is a dummy suffix on the same level (both on the bottom), which is not allowed in a generalised coordinate systems. Same for (3) and (4). Notice that (3) also is missing an r on the right-hand side.

3 6.4 Given a Cartesian coordinate system K with orthonormal basis i1, i2, i3, consider the second-order tensor with components [Pik] = [P ik] = [P .k i ] = [P i .k] =   1 1 −1 2 3 0 0 −2 1   . Let K′ be a new coordinate system with basis vectors e1 = i1, e2 = i1 − i2, e3 = i1 + i2 + 2i3. (1) Compute the dual basis vectors e1, e2, e3. (2) Using (1) where possible, express the covariant, contravariant and mixed components of the given tensor in the system K′. Solution: (1) Using the dual basis formula (check previous practical sheets if needed), we obtain: e 1 =   1 1 −1   , e 2 =   0 −1 1/2   , e 3 =   0 0 1/2   . (2) We have P ′ ik = L ℓ i′L m k′ Pℓm, where Lp q′ = eq · ip are the coefficients of the direct transformation above, i.e., L 1 1′ = 1, L 2 1′ = 0, L 3 1′ = 0, L 1 2′ = 1, L 2 2′ = −1, L 3 2′ = 0, L 1 3′ = 1, L 2 3′ = 1, L 3 3′ = 2. For instance, L 1 3′ = e3 · i1 = (i1 + i2 + 2i3) · i1 = 1. To compute [P ′ ik], we use the formula P ′ ik = L ℓ i′L m k′ Pℓm. If we had to use the definition, we would have for instance, P ′ 23 = L ℓ 2′L m 3′ Pℓm = 3∑ ℓ=1 3∑ m=1 L ℓ 2′L m 3′ Pℓm, which is a lot of work. So, instead, we can define the matrix L = [Li j′] (and write P = [Pℓm]) and notice that (LP )im = (L)iℓ(P )ℓm = Lℓ i′Pℓm.

Hence, we only need to perform matrix multiplications: P ′ = [P ′ ik] = LP L T =   1 0 0 1 −1 0 1 1 2   ·  1 1 −1 2 3 0 0 −2 1   ·   1 0 0 1 −1 0 1 1 2   T =   1 1 −1 −1 −2 −1 3 0 1   ·  1 1 1 0 −1 1 0 0 2   =   1 0 0 −1 1 −5 3 3 5   . To find P ′ik, P ′.k i and P ′i .k, we use the formulae P ′ik = giℓgkmP ′ ℓm, P ′.k i = gkℓP ′ iℓ, P ′i .k = giℓP ′ ℓk, Writing G for the matrix defined by gpq and recalling that gpq = gqp, we rewrite the about suffix notation equations in matrix form: P ′ik = giℓP ′ ℓmgmk = (GP ′G)ik, P ′.k i = P ′ iℓgℓk = (P ′G)ik, P ′i .k = giℓP ′ ℓk = (GP ′)ik. First note that G = [gik] = [e i · e k] =   3 −3/2 −1/2 −3/2 5/4 1/4 −1/2 1/4 1/4   .

(2) The matrix L = [Li j′] is given by the identity L p q′ = eq · ip: L =  L1 1′ L2 1′ L3 1′ L1 2′ L2 2′ L3 2′ L1 3′ L2 3′ L3 3′   =   1 −1 0 0 1 0 1 0 2   . To find P ′ik, P ′.k i and P ′i .k, we use the formulae P ′ik = giℓgkmP ′ ℓm, P ′.k i = gkℓP ′ iℓ, P ′i .k = giℓP ′ ℓk, Writing G for the matrix defined by gpq and recalling that gpq = gqp, we rewrite the about suffix notation equations in matrix form: P ′ik = giℓP ′ ℓmgmk = (GP ′G)ik, P ′.k i = P ′ iℓgℓk = (P ′G)ik, P ′i .k = giℓP ′ ℓk = (GP ′)ik. First note that G = [gik] = [e i · e k] =   5/4 5/4 −1/4 5/4 9/4 −1/4 −1/4 −1/4 1/4   .

8 Solution: (1) We need to find the matrix L = (L j i′) satisfying  e1 e2 e3   = L  i1 i2 i3   . We see that L =  1 −1 0 1 4 1 1 3 1   . We know that the covariant components of B are given by B′ ik = Lℓ i′Lm k′ Bℓm = [LBLT ]ik, so we only need to compute LBLT : B ′ = LBL T =  1 −1 0 1 4 1 1 3 1     0 1 0 −1 0 1 0 0 1     1 −1 0 1 4 1 1 3 1   T =   1 1 −1 −4 1 5 −3 1 4     1 1 1 −1 4 3 0 1 1   =   0 4 3 −5 5 4 −4 5 4   (2) Using the dual basis formula, we obtain: e 1 =   1 0 −1   , e 2 =   1 1 −4   , e 3 =  −1 −1 5   . (3) To find B′ik, B′·k i and B′i ·k, we use the formulae B′ik = giℓgkmB′ ℓm, B′·k i = gkℓB′ iℓ, B′i ·k = giℓB′ ℓk, Writing G for the matrix defined by gpq and recalling that gpq = gqp, we rewrite the about suffix notation equations in matrix form: B′ik = giℓB′ ℓmgmk = (GB ′G)ik, B′·k i = B′ iℓgℓk = (B ′G)ik, B′i ·k = giℓB′ ℓk = (GB ′)ik.
